analysis.one_liner: Requires crash-data recorders in all new vehicles, readable by any owner.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by one senator with no cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, got a single hearing in May 2010, and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every new car, truck, and heavy vehicle sold in the United States to carry an event data recorder — the "black box" that stores what happened in a crash — and required that the data be retrievable with a standard, commercially available reader rather than manufacturer-only tools. It included privacy rules: only the vehicle owner, a court, or a safety agency (with personal details stripped) could pull the data. Its stated goal was better crash investigation and safer vehicle design, building on safety regulators' own findings about recorders.
analysis.who_benefits: Car buyers, crash victims and their families, safety researchers and crash investigators. Investigators get standardized, retrievable crash data to pinpoint causes; the bill's findings cite regulator research that awareness of a recorder reduces crash severity, and open access to non-personal data helps engineers fix defects. The privacy clause also protects owners' personal data.

how_it_helps.text: Requires event data recorders in every new light-duty vehicle and, on a longer timetable, medium- and heavy-duty vehicles, with the data accessible by a commercially available universal reader instead of proprietary manufacturer-only tools [S3][S2].

Requires owner's manuals to clearly disclose the presence of a recorder, and bars anyone but the owner from retrieving the data without court authorization, owner consent, or an anonymized safety-agency retrieval [S3][S2].

The bill's own findings cite a federal working group's conclusion that event data recorders can improve occupant protection systems and crash reconstruction, and that driver awareness of an onboard recorder reduces the number and severity of crashes [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Vehicle manufacturers, who would bear the cost of installing compliant recorders in every vehicle and opening their proprietary data formats to universal readers; some of that cost would likely be passed to buyers through vehicle prices.

drawbacks.text: A mandated recorder documents a driver's speed, braking, and behavior in the moments before a crash, which insurers, police, and opposing lawyers could seek or argue over even with the bill's consent and court-order limits; some drivers would reasonably see this as surveillance in their own vehicles [S3].
Mandated hardware adds compliance costs for manufacturers on a mandate covering every new vehicle sold, a cost that would partly surface in vehicle prices [S3].
Requiring a universal data reader erodes manufacturers' control over proprietary vehicle data, a real business interest even if framed as a safety gain [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill paired a modest hardware mandate with unusually strong privacy limits and disclosure rules, so the main honest objection is the price tag and the surveillance discomfort, not design flaws. By 2010 many light vehicles already had recorders voluntarily, so the bill largely would have standardized what already existed and extended it to heavier vehicles; its cost to manufacturers was real but small relative to vehicle prices. A reasonable bill that died from inattention rather than merit.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which held one hearing in May 2010, and then it simply sat there until the Congress ended in January 2011, never reaching a committee vote or the Senate floor [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Senator Tom Udall introduced the bill on April 28, 2010; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day [S5][S1].
The committee held hearings on May 19, 2010, the only action after referral; the bill was never reported out or voted on in either chamber before the 111th Congress ended [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers were better off: no federal mandate to install recorders in every vehicle or open proprietary crash data to universal readers took effect. Drivers and insurers also kept the status quo of recorder use, where data access is governed by older, narrower rules rather than the bill's nationwide standard.

for.name: Sen. Tom Udall
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; the only senator supporting it on the record.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee of referral (full committee held hearings)
against.what_they_did: Held a hearing on May 19, 2010, then took no further action; never reported the bill, so it never got a committee vote or a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no opposition is on the record, so the partisan shape cannot be measured; the bill simply had one sponsor and no cosponsors [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have required recorders in every new vehicle and opened manufacturers' proprietary crash-data formats to universal readers, a compliance and data-control cost. Most manufacturers already installed recorders in many light vehicles voluntarily, so the mandate mainly standardized the fleet, but heavier vehicles and universal readers were new costs.

Standardized retrievable crash data would make fault analysis easier and cheaper for insurers and investigators. But data access is precisely where an industry interest can diverge from a driver's: the bill's privacy clause would have restricted who could pull the data, cutting off the freest access the industry enjoys today under the status quo.
